episodes.title: Time, Compressed
episodes.subject: Time
episodes.hook: We have saved more time than any generation in history. So why does every one of us feel like we are running out of it?
episodes.question: Did you know that time itself has been compressing for five hundred years?
episodes.guess: Where did all the time we saved actually go? Write your guess in the comments before you press play.
episodes.summary: Seven centuries, seven mornings: from a village that wakes at midnight to a phone checked before your feet touch the floor — and what the year 2100 is about to take next.

quiz.question: Did time really speed up over 500 years?
options: No — we pack more into it and remember less
quiz.reveal: A second in 1500 lasted exactly as long as one today. What changed is how much we pack into it — and how little we remember.

questions.question: In 1500, how did many people sleep?
options: In two parts: a “first sleep” and a “second sleep”
Only in the afternoon, after lunch
Never more than four hours a night
Sitting up, so they would wake at dawn
questions.reveal: Historians have found hundreds of references to a “first sleep” and a “second sleep”. In between, people prayed, talked — even visited neighbours.

questions.question: What were England’s first coffeehouses nicknamed?
questions.reveal: For one penny you could walk in, read the news and argue with strangers for hours — London’s first coffeehouse opened in 1652.

questions.question: Workers in the 1700s often took one day off that was not Sunday. What did they call it?
questions.reveal: For generations, workers simply took Mondays off — “Saint Monday”. Factory clocks slowly made it disappear.

questions.question: How did the weekend begin?
options: With a free Friday for farmers
With half a Saturday: mill work ended at 2 p.m.
With a week off every summer
questions.reveal: An 1850 British law ended mill work for women and children at 2 p.m. on Saturdays. Soon the men got the same — even free time had to be written into law.

questions.question: On 18 November 1883, some American towns heard noon twice. Why?
options: The railroads switched to standard time zones
The Sun seemed to stop in the sky
A new law moved noon to 1 p.m.
questions.reveal: The railroads reset the clocks of a whole continent to standard time zones — the “Day of Two Noons”.

questions.question: What did Henry Ford offer his workers in 1914?
options: $5 a day for an eight-hour day
A free Model T every year
$1 a day for a twelve-hour day
questions.reveal: Ford more than doubled pay, to $5 a day, and cut the day to eight hours. By 1926 his workers had Saturdays off too.

questions.question: How long does the average internet user spend online every day?
questions.reveal: Adult internet users average 6 hours 38 minutes online — every single day.

questions.question: So where did all the time we saved go?
options: Clocks tick faster than they did in 1500
We pack more into every hour — and remember less of it
Days are shorter than they used to be
questions.reveal: A second in 1500 lasted exactly as long as one today. Your brain measures time with new memories — so hours that all look the same seem to vanish.

eras.line: It is midnight. Pitch black. And the whole village is awake.
eras.saw: Your day begins when the sun rises, and ends when it sets. The church bell is the only clock you will ever hear.

eras.line: The air smells of smoke — and of something new.
eras.saw: His drifts by seconds. For the first time, an ordinary day can be cut into minutes.

eras.line: Monday morning, and half the workshop is empty.
eras.saw: Time is now something you can carry. And something you can sell.

eras.line: At midday the church clock strikes twelve. Then it is noon again.
eras.saw: The railroads had reset the clocks of an entire continent.

eras.line: The line of people looking for work stretches down the street.
eras.saw: Henry Ford more than doubled his workers’ pay, to five dollars a day, and cut the day to eight hours.

eras.line: Before your feet touch the floor, you have already checked your phone.
eras.saw: On paper, we are the richest people in history, rich in time. And yet, ask anyone how they are, and you will hear the same word. Busy.

eras.line: That morning has not happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: It could finally arrive, a century late. But if history repeats, we will fill every freed hour with something faster.

facts.fact: For centuries, people slept twice a night. Historians have found hundreds of references to a “first sleep” and a “second sleep”.
facts.source: A. Roger Ekirch, At Day’s Close (2005)

facts.fact: England’s first coffeehouses were nicknamed “penny universities”: one penny bought coffee, the news and hours of argument with strangers.
facts.source: Historic UK · English coffeehouses

facts.fact: For generations, workers simply took Mondays off. They called it “Saint Monday”.
facts.source: E. P. Thompson, Past & Present 38 (1967)

facts.fact: The weekend began with half a Saturday: an 1850 British law ended mill work for women and children at 2 p.m. on Saturdays.
facts.source: Factory Act 1850

facts.fact: On 18 November 1883, American and Canadian railroads switched to standard time zones. Some towns heard noon twice that day — the “Day of Two Noons”.
facts.source: Chicago Public Library · The Day of Two Noons

facts.fact: Henry Ford more than doubled his workers’ pay, to $5 a day — and cut the working day to eight hours.
facts.source: The Henry Ford

facts.fact: The average internet user now spends 6 hours 38 minutes online, every single day.
facts.source: DataReportal, Digital 2025

facts.fact: Your brain measures time with memories, not clocks. A week full of new experiences feels long when you look back; months of routine shrink to almost nothing. Psychologists call it the holiday paradox.
facts.source: Claudia Hammond, Time Warped (2012)

episodes.commentPrompt: If you could wake up in any century, from 1500 to 2100, which would you choose — and why?

episodes.title: The Sun
episodes.subject: The Sun
episodes.hook: Every time you look at the Sun, you are looking into the past.
episodes.question: Did you know that you have never once seen the Sun as it is right now?
episodes.guess: That light on your face is eight minutes old. But the energy inside it — how old is that? Guess in the comments, then stay to the end and check.
episodes.summary: Seven mornings under the same Sun, and one relationship that climbs rung by rung: Midsummer bonfires in Tudor London, the first telescope drawing of sunspots, leaves that bubble in sunlight, Herschel’s invisible light, the suntan myth, solar power almost eleven times bigger in ten years — and a 2100 scenario, clearly labelled, where the Sun might decide whether your AI wakes up.

quiz.question: How old is the sunlight hitting your eyes right now?
quiz.reveal: Sunlight needs about 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross the average Earth–Sun distance — and the energy in it was made in the Sun’s core long before that (NASA estimates about 170,000 years). You have never seen the Sun as it is — only as it was.

questions.question: In 1500, what did almost everyone believe about the Sun?
options: That it goes around the Earth
That it is a bonfire in the sky
That it is made of iron
That it stands still at the centre
questions.reveal: It is what Ptolemy had taught, about 1,400 years earlier. In 1543, the year he died, Copernicus’s book put the Sun at the centre instead.

questions.question: Who made the first telescope drawing of sunspots?
options: Thomas Harriot, beside the River Thames
questions.reveal: On a misty December morning in 1610, the Englishman Thomas Harriot pointed a telescope at the low Sun and drew what he saw — and never published it. Galileo’s letters on the spots came out in 1613.

questions.question: In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz sank leaves under water. What did he see in sunlight?
options: They bubbled out fresh air — and stopped in the shade
questions.reveal: In more than 500 experiments he found that only the green parts do it, and only in light. Plants need the Sun.

questions.question: In 1800, William Herschel put thermometers in a rainbow made by a prism. Where was the hottest spot?
options: In the yellow, the brightest colour
Just past the red, where nothing was visible
questions.reveal: The reading beyond the red was the highest of all. Herschel had found infrared — the Sun was sending more than our eyes could catch.

questions.question: How leaves turn sunlight into sugar got its name in 1893. What is it called?
questions.reveal: The name is usually credited to the American botanist Charles Reid Barnes. Nearly all life runs on it — your lunch is stored sunlight.

questions.question: The famous story says Coco Chanel started the suntan craze. What did a historian find?
options: It is true — she returned tanned from a cruise in 1923
It is probably a myth, traced to an unsigned magazine article from 1971
It was actually her rival Elsa Schiaparelli
Tanning was banned in France until 1930
questions.reveal: Kerry Segrave traced the Chanel story to an unsigned 1971 magazine article; tanning was already a fad before 1920. The real reason was work: as jobs moved indoors, a tan became the badge of leisure.

questions.question: In 2025, how much electricity did solar power make compared with ten years earlier?
questions.reveal: About 2,770 TWh in 2025 against about 250 TWh in 2015 — almost nine percent of all the world’s electricity.

questions.question: So how old is the sunlight hitting your face right now?
options: About 8 minutes 20 seconds — and its energy left the Sun’s core long before that
questions.reveal: Light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross 150 million km. But the energy in it was made in the Sun’s core and spent a very long time struggling out — NASA estimates about 170,000 years. When it began its journey there were no farms, no cities and no writing.

eras.line: It is Midsummer Eve, and the streets are glowing with firelight.
eras.saw: It’s the difference between day and night. Daylight is for work. Darkness is for sleep, and prayer.

eras.line: A misty December morning. The Sun hangs low and dim — and a man points a telescope at it.
eras.saw: For a few people with telescopes, the Sun has become something to watch. Closely.

eras.line: A bright summer morning, and the fashionable ladies are hiding from the Sun under parasols.
eras.saw: This summer, the Sun is turning into something new. Something to explain.

eras.line: An astronomer has set a prism in a sunbeam, with thermometers whose bulbs are blackened.
eras.saw: Now the Sun is something you measure, even where your eyes give up.

eras.line: Hot sand. Salt air. And everyone is lying in the Sun, on purpose.
eras.saw: The Sun used to be something to measure. Now, it’s the source of every meal.

eras.line: Your phone’s charged, the lights come on — and a field of solar panels has been awake since sunrise.
eras.saw: So what’s the Sun to you now? Power. Something you harvest, like a crop.

eras.line: That morning has not happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: In 1500, the Sun decided when you went to sleep. In 2100, it might decide whether your AI wakes up.

facts.fact: In 1500, almost everyone believed the Sun goes around the Earth — what Ptolemy had taught about 1,400 years earlier. In 1543, the year he died, Copernicus’s book put the Sun at the centre.
facts.source: Copernicus, De revolutionibus (1543)

facts.fact: The first telescope drawing of sunspots was made on 8 December 1610 by the Englishman Thomas Harriot, beside the Thames — not by Galileo, who published his letters on the spots in 1613. Harriot never published his.
facts.source: HAO/UCAR · Galileo, Letters on Sunspots (1613)

facts.fact: In the summer of 1779, the Dutch doctor Jan Ingenhousz ran more than 500 experiments on plants. Leaves sunk in water bubbled out fresh air in sunlight and stopped in the shade — and only the green parts did it.
facts.source: Jan Ingenhousz, Experiments upon Vegetables (1779)

facts.fact: William Herschel set a prism in a sunbeam and found the hottest spot just past the red, where nothing was visible. He had found infrared: the Sun sends more than our eyes can catch.
facts.source: NASA Space Place · Caltech IPAC

facts.fact: Leaves catch sunlight and turn it into sugar, and nearly all life runs on that. The process got its name in 1893 — photosynthesis — usually credited to the American botanist Charles Reid Barnes.
facts.source: Etymonline · Charles Reid Barnes (1893)

facts.fact: The story that Coco Chanel started the suntan craze is probably a myth: a historian traced it to an unsigned 1971 magazine article. As work moved indoors, a tan became the badge of leisure.
facts.source: Kerry Segrave, Suntanning in 20th Century America (2005)

facts.fact: In 2025, solar power made almost eleven times more electricity than ten years earlier: about 2,770 TWh, against about 250 TWh in 2015. That is almost 9% of all the world’s electricity.
facts.source: Ember, Global Electricity Review 2026

facts.fact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach you. But the energy in it was made in the Sun’s core and took a very long time to get out — NASA estimates about 170,000 years. You have never seen the Sun as it is. Only as it was.
facts.source: NASA · Sun facts

episodes.commentPrompt: In which century would you rather watch the Sun rise?

episodes.title: School
episodes.subject: School
episodes.hook: Five hundred years ago, most children never saw a classroom. They worked.
episodes.question: Did you know that the word “school” first meant the one thing school seems to take away from you?
episodes.guess: Two hundred years ago, out of every ten people on Earth, how many could read? Guess in the comments, then stay to the end and check.
episodes.summary: Seven mornings, seven school days — or days with no school at all: a prince with his own tutor in Tudor London, a 1647 law that begins by blaming the devil, the Prussian law that banned school holidays, Joseph Lancaster’s thousand-pupil schools and their cages, the high-school boom and a right to education for everyone, the 2020 closures — and a 2100 scenario, clearly labelled, where every child might have a tutor.

quiz.question: Two hundred years ago, out of every ten people on Earth, how many could read?
quiz.reveal: About one in ten: historians estimate about 12% of the world could read in 1820. Today it is almost nine in ten — 87% of adults in 2022.

questions.question: In 1500, who taught nine-year-old Prince Henry, the future Henry VIII?
options: A village priest, with forty other boys
The poet John Skelton — a teacher all to himself
Nobody — princes did not learn to read
questions.reveal: One teacher, one child. Most children learned by working — a craftsman’s son was usually apprenticed for seven years — but a prince had the poet John Skelton all to himself.

questions.question: How does one of America’s first school laws, from Massachusetts in 1647, begin?
options: By thanking the King of England
With a list of fines for lazy pupils
questions.reveal: It calls keeping people from the Scriptures a chief project of “that old deluder, Satan”. Any town with fifty households had to hire someone to teach reading and writing.

questions.question: What did Frederick the Great’s 1763 school law in Prussia ban?
options: School holidays — not even at harvest time
questions.reveal: “No vacations are to be given, not even during harvest time.” Every boy and girl was to go from five until about thirteen — though plenty of families just ignored the rules.

questions.question: Joseph Lancaster claimed one master could run a school of how many children?
questions.reveal: His trick: older children taught the younger ones in small groups. Pupils wrote letters in sand because paper cost money — and a misbehaving child might be hoisted up in a cage.

questions.question: In 1880, school became compulsory in England. For which ages?
questions.reveal: From five to ten. Fees were still charged until 1891, when school became free for most families.

questions.question: In December 1948, in Paris, the United Nations wrote down for the whole world that everyone has the right to…
options: Education — free, at least in the early years
questions.reveal: Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: “Everyone has the right to education.” Free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages.

questions.question: In April 2020, about how many learners were sent home as schools closed?
options: About 1.6 billion — more than nine in ten students on Earth
questions.reveal: UNESCO counted more than 1.6 billion learners out of school at the peak, in over 190 countries. Lessons moved into kitchens and bedrooms.

questions.question: “School” comes from the ancient Greek word scholé. What did it first mean?
questions.reveal: In Athens, people with free time often spent it talking, arguing and learning — so the word for leisure became the word for learned talk, and then for the place you learn.

eras.line: It’s still dark. Next door, a hammer’s already going, and the street smells of wet straw and wood smoke.
eras.saw: Something for other people. For priests, and rich boys. Most children learn by working.

eras.line: There’s frost on the window, and the cows need milking before breakfast.
eras.saw: A way to read God’s word, with your own eyes.

eras.line: It’s autumn. The war’s just over, the harvest’s in, and the pastor has news from the king.
eras.saw: An order. From the king.

eras.line: One enormous hall. Hundreds of children, in long rows. And just one master.
eras.saw: A machine. For teaching the poor, by the hundred, as cheaply as possible.

eras.line: It’s June. Graduation day. Your mum’s ironing your gown, and the radio’s on.
eras.saw: So now school is a right. And a ladder. And a building you walk to every morning.

eras.line: Your phone buzzes. Homework’s due at midnight. And any question you’ve got, you can ask a screen.
eras.saw: Always on. A classroom, plus a screen that never closes.

eras.line: That morning hasn’t happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: In 1500, a private teacher was for a prince. In 2100, it might be for everyone.

facts.fact: In 1500, nine-year-old Prince Henry — the future Henry VIII — had a teacher all to himself: the poet John Skelton. Most children learned by working, and historians estimate only about one woman in a hundred in England could even write her own name.
facts.source: EBSCO · Luminarium (Skelton) · David Cressy, Literacy and the Social Order (1980)

facts.fact: One of America’s first school laws, Massachusetts 1647, begins by blaming “that old deluder, Satan”. Any town with fifty households had to hire someone to teach reading and writing; a hundred households, a grammar school too — or the town paid a fine.
facts.source: Massachusetts Archives · Records of the Massachusetts Bay (1853)

facts.fact: Frederick the Great’s 1763 school law banned school holidays — “not even during harvest time”. Every boy and girl was to go from five until about thirteen, and parents of children who skipped could be fined.
facts.source: Prussian General School Regulation, 12 Aug 1763 (GHDI)

facts.fact: Joseph Lancaster claimed one master could run a school of more than a thousand children, with older pupils teaching the younger ones. Misbehave, and you might be hoisted above the classroom in a cage — he thought it beat the cane.
facts.source: Joseph Lancaster, Improvements in Education (1803) · Dictionary of Canadian Biography

facts.fact: In 1880, school became compulsory in England for children from five to ten. Fees were still charged until 1891, when school became free for most families.
facts.source: UK Parliament, Living Heritage: the 1870 Education Act

facts.fact: On 10 December 1948, in Paris, the United Nations wrote it down for the whole world: “Everyone has the right to education.” Free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages.
facts.source: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 26

facts.fact: In April 2020, about 1.6 billion learners were sent home as schools closed — more than nine in ten students on Earth. At least 463 million children could not get remote lessons at all.
facts.source: UNESCO COVID-19 education monitoring (2020) · UNICEF, Remote Learning Reachability (2020)

facts.fact: “School” comes from the ancient Greek scholé, which meant free time — leisure. In Athens, people with free time often spent it in discussion, so the word for leisure became the word for the place you learn. And literacy? About one in ten could read in 1820; today it is almost nine in ten.
facts.source: Liddell–Scott–Jones Greek Lexicon · Our World in Data, Literacy

episodes.title: Money
episodes.subject: Money
keywords: i promise to pay the bearer
episodes.hook: Most money today isn’t paper, or metal, or anything you could ever hold. So what is it?
episodes.question: Did you know that one word printed on every Bank of England note tells you what money really is?
episodes.guess: In Britain, out of every hundred pounds people have, how many exist as real notes and coins? Guess in the comments, then stay to the end and check.
episodes.summary: Seven mornings, seven kinds of money: cacao beans in Tenochtitlan’s market (and the sellers who faked them), Sweden’s 20-kilo copper coin and Europe’s first real banknotes, John Law’s Paris and the Mississippi bubble, the Bank of England’s printed promise, the August evening in 1971 when the dollar’s link to gold was cut, mobile money in Nairobi — and a 2100 scenario, clearly labelled, where money might be written in code.

quiz.question: In Britain, out of every hundred pounds people have, how many exist as real notes and coins?
quiz.reveal: About three. When the Bank of England checked, in 2014, about 97 of every 100 pounds were bank deposits — only about 3 were notes and coins.

questions.question: Aztec money grew on trees: cacao beans. A price list from a few decades later (Tlaxcala, 1545) says a good turkey hen cost how many beans?
questions.reveal: A hundred — and one ripe avocado cost a single bean. Bigger deals were paid in cotton cloaks, and a Spanish friar wrote about sellers who faked cacao beans.

questions.question: In 1661, a Stockholm bank handed out Europe’s first real banknotes. Why was paper such a relief in Sweden?
options: Sweden’s biggest coin was a copper plate weighing almost 20 kilos
The king had banned metal coins
Sweden had run out of copper
questions.reveal: The biggest plate weighed 19.7 kg — you needed a cart, not a pocket. Johan Palmstruch’s bank lent out paper notes instead, promising to pay them in coin on demand: a promise, written on paper.

questions.question: In February 1720, what did France make illegal?
options: Owning more than 500 livres in gold or silver
questions.reveal: The government wanted people to trust John Law’s paper — by law. Shares in his Mississippi Company had gone up about forty times; by December they had crashed, and Law escaped France.

questions.question: Bank of England notes still say “I promise to pay the bearer on demand”. In 1821, what could a £5 note be swapped for?
options: Nothing — it was just a saying
questions.reveal: Five gold sovereigns: back then, the promise meant gold. Today it only means another Bank of England note — there has been no gold link since 1931.

questions.question: From 1933, what was illegal for most Americans to own?
questions.reveal: Gold coins or bars, with a few exceptions such as jewellery and collectors’ coins. The ban lasted until the end of 1974 — so in 1971, most Americans couldn’t own gold at all.

questions.question: On a Sunday evening in August 1971, President Nixon said foreign governments could no longer swap their dollars for…
questions.reveal: Since 1944, governments could swap dollars for American gold at $35 an ounce. Within a few years the whole system was gone: money became a promise backed by trust.

questions.question: About how many adults in Kenya use mobile money today?
questions.reveal: About eight in ten — 82% in 2024, up from 28% in 2009. M-Pesa launched in 2007, and school fees and taxi rides now get paid with a text.

questions.question: The Bank of England puts it plainly. Money today is a type of…
options: IOU — a promise everyone trusts others will accept
questions.reveal: A special kind of IOU, trusted because everyone expects others to accept it. Remember the word from Stockholm? Promise. It was there all along.

eras.line: Canoes bump along the canals. The market’s already loud, and it smells of chilli and wood smoke.
eras.saw: Something useful. Something you could even drink.

eras.line: The harbour’s frozen, and a sledge scrapes past your window, loaded with copper.
eras.saw: A promise. Written on paper.

eras.line: The street smells of horses, and everyone’s talking about paper.
eras.saw: A belief. It’s worth whatever everyone believes it’s worth. Until they don’t.

eras.line: Coal smoke, wet cobbles, and a queue outside the Bank of England.
eras.saw: As good as gold. A promise you can swap for metal.

eras.line: It’s a Sunday evening in August, and the whole family’s in front of the TV.
eras.saw: A promise backed by trust. Trust in the people who run it.

eras.line: Matatus honk on the road outside, and your phone buzzes. Your sister just sent you money. It took seconds.
eras.saw: Numbers on a screen. You almost never touch it.

eras.line: That morning hasn’t happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: In 1500, money grew on trees. In 2100, it might be written in code — but it would still be a promise.

facts.fact: In Tenochtitlan, money grew on trees: cacao beans, the beans that make chocolate. A price list from a few decades later says one ripe avocado cost one bean and a good turkey hen a hundred — and a Spanish friar wrote about sellers who faked cacao beans.
facts.source: Cornell University Library, Chocolate: Food of the Gods · Tlaxcala price list, 1545 (Beyond the Codices, 1976) · Florentine Codex, Book 10

facts.fact: Sweden’s biggest coin was a copper plate weighing 19.7 kg. In 1661 Johan Palmstruch’s Stockholms Banco issued paper instead — the first real banknotes in Europe. It printed and lent more than it had copper, failed, and Palmstruch was sentenced to death. He was spared.
facts.source: Sveriges Riksbank, historical timeline · NY Fed Liberty Street Economics (2013)

facts.fact: On 27 February 1720, France made it illegal to own more than 500 livres in gold or silver. John Law’s Mississippi Company shares had gone up about forty times; by December they had crashed, and Law escaped France.
facts.source: François Velde, Government Equity and Money (Chicago Fed WP 2003-31) · Britannica Money, John Law

facts.fact: Bank of England notes still say “I promise to pay the bearer on demand”. In 1821 that promise meant gold: a £5 note could be swapped for five gold sovereigns, after 24 years in which the Bank had stopped paying out gold.
facts.source: Bank of England, Banknote FAQs · Bank Restriction Act 1797

facts.fact: From 1933, it was illegal for most Americans to own gold coins or bars — and it stayed illegal until the end of 1974.
facts.source: Executive Order 6102 (1933) · Public Law 93-373

facts.fact: On the evening of 15 August 1971, President Nixon ended foreign governments’ right to swap their dollars for American gold at $35 an ounce, the rate set at Bretton Woods in 1944. Within a few years, the whole system was gone.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Nixon Ends Convertibility of U.S. Dollars to Gold

facts.fact: About eight in ten adults in Kenya use mobile money — 82% in 2024, up from 28% in 2009; M-Pesa launched in 2007. Across the euro area, cash paid for 79% of shop purchases in 2016 and 52% in 2024.
facts.source: FSD Kenya, 2024 FinAccess Household Survey · ECB, SPACE 2024

facts.fact: The Bank of England calls money today a special kind of IOU, trusted because everyone expects others to accept it. When it checked, in 2014, about 97 of every 100 pounds were bank deposits and only about 3 were notes and coins — and, within limits, a bank loan creates a new deposit.
facts.source: Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1 (McLeay, Radia & Thomas)

episodes.title: Food
episodes.subject: Food
episodes.hook: About one in five deaths around the world is linked to diet. So did food give us our longer lives — or is it taking some of those years back?
episodes.question: Did you know that today, about one in five deaths around the world is linked to diet?
episodes.guess: In 1800, life expectancy at birth, worldwide, was about 29 years. What about a baby born today? Guess in the comments, then stay to the end and check.
episodes.summary: Seven mornings, seven plates: bread and dried fish on a Flemish fast day, ship’s biscuit and James Lind’s oranges and lemons on a British warship, white rice and beriberi on a Japanese training ship, the Mississippi prison farm where pellagra was traced to diet, the new wheat in Punjab, rice and beans and a delivery app in São Paulo — and a 2100 scenario, clearly labelled, where the average life could stretch past eighty.

quiz.question: In 1800, life expectancy at birth, worldwide, was about 29 years. What is it for a baby born today?
quiz.reveal: About seventy three: 73.3 years worldwide in 2024, says the UN. Every one of these figures is an average at birth, pulled down by the children who died young.

questions.question: In a Flemish village in 1500, on up to how many days in ten was eating meat against the Church’s rules?
questions.reveal: Up to four in ten: Fridays, Lent, Advent — the fast days, when fish took meat’s place. Bread came at almost every meal, and food took 70–80% of what a family spent.

questions.question: Aboard HMS Salisbury in 1747, James Lind gave six pairs of sailors with scurvy something different each. Which pair did best?
options: The pair given two oranges and a lemon a day
questions.reveal: Oranges and a lemon. The fruit ran out after six days, and by then one of that pair was fit for duty. Lind didn’t know why it worked — but the right food could cure you.

questions.question: Lind found his cure in 1747. When did the Royal Navy finally hand out lemon juice to its sailors?
questions.reveal: In 1795, 48 years after Lind’s trial. Meanwhile, on land in Britain, a newborn could still expect fewer than forty years.

questions.question: Japanese sailors lived almost entirely on white rice and kept getting beriberi. In 1884, after Takaki Kanehiro changed the menu, how many men on the training ship Tsukuba died of it?
questions.reveal: None. Fourteen got sick — and they hadn’t eaten the new food. The year before, on the Ryujo, 169 men got beriberi and 25 died. Decades later, the missing piece got a name: a vitamin.

questions.question: In 1915, on a Mississippi prison farm, healthy volunteers were promised a pardon. What did doctors ask them to do?
options: Eat a poor Southern family’s ordinary diet
Work double shifts in the fields
questions.reveal: Cornbread and grits, fatty salt pork, molasses — hardly any milk, fresh meat or greens. After about five months, around half of the men had pellagra. It wasn’t a germ: something was missing from the diet.

questions.question: In 1965, with war and drought leaving too little grain, what did India’s prime minister ask the whole country to do?
options: Give up sugar for a year
questions.reveal: Skip one meal a week — Lal Bahadur Shastri’s appeal. Then India imported 18,000 tonnes of Mexican wheat seed, and within a few years its wheat harvest jumped to 17 million tonnes.

questions.question: In Brazil, ultra-processed food is about a fifth of the calories people eat. What about in the United States?
questions.reveal: More than half. Brazil’s food guide has a golden rule: choose fresh food and home-made meals over ultra-processed food.

questions.question: One study of big American cities in the early 1900s found a single change behind nearly half the drop in deaths. What was it?
questions.reveal: Clean water. Food gave us years, but not alone: sewers, vaccines and medicine did much of the rest. And today, about one in five deaths worldwide is linked to diet.

eras.line: The bread oven’s warm, and the kitchen smells of rye and smoke.
eras.saw: Fuel. Enough to survive the day.

eras.line: A British warship on patrol. Every day: hard biscuit, beer, and almost nothing fresh.
eras.saw: Medicine. The right food can cure you.

eras.line: A training ship called the Tsukuba is getting ready to sail.
eras.saw: Something to measure. What’s inside it matters.

eras.line: Eleven men are lining up for breakfast.
eras.saw: Something we fix. Add what’s missing, and a disease disappears.

eras.line: Everyone’s watching the sky for rain.
eras.saw: Enough, at last. Grown by the tonne.

eras.line: Motorbikes buzz past with food deliveries.
eras.saw: Too much of some things. Too little of others.

eras.line: That morning hasn’t happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: In 1500, the Church decided which days you couldn’t eat meat. In 2100, the reason might be your heart — and the planet.

facts.fact: In Flanders around 1500, eating meat was against the Church’s rules on up to four days in ten: Fridays, Lent, Advent. Bread came at almost every meal, with porridge, peas and beans, beer, and dried fish on fast days — and food took 70–80% of what a family spent. In England next door, a newborn could expect about 35 years, mostly because so many children died.
facts.source: Fitzwilliam Museum, Feast & Fast · Rose, “Low Countries”, Encyclopedia of Food and Culture · Munro 2003 · Wrigley & Schofield, via Our World in Data

facts.fact: On 20 May 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, the surgeon James Lind split twelve sailors with scurvy into six pairs. The pair given two oranges and a lemon a day did best: one man was fit for duty after six days. The navy’s daily ration was a pound of hard biscuit and a gallon of beer, with almost nothing fresh.
facts.source: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753), via the James Lind Library · Royal Navy victualling scale (University of Greenwich)

facts.fact: The Royal Navy ordered lemon juice for all its sailors in 1795 — 48 years after Lind’s trial. On land in Britain, a newborn in 1748 could expect about 36 years.
facts.source: Dictionary of National Biography, “Blane, Gilbert” · Wrigley & Schofield series, via Our World in Data

facts.fact: On the Japanese navy ship Ryujo in 1882–83, 169 of 376 men got beriberi and 25 died; sailors ate almost nothing but white rice. Takaki Kanehiro changed the menu — more barley, meat, milk, bread and vegetables — and on the Tsukuba in 1884, 14 men got sick and none died. Japanese men born in 1896 were about 15 cm shorter than men born in 1996.
facts.source: James Lind Library, Kanehiro Takaki · Sugiyama & Seita, JRSM (2013) · NCD-RisC, eLife (2016)

facts.fact: In 1915, at a prison farm in Mississippi, Joseph Goldberger fed healthy volunteers, promised a pardon, a poor Southern family’s ordinary corn-based diet. After about five months, around half of the eleven men had pellagra. The missing nutrient, niacin, was added to flour and bread across much of America in the 1940s.
facts.source: Goldberger & Wheeler, Public Health Reports (1915) · Encyclopedia of Arkansas, Pellagra · Clay, Schmick & Troesken (2019)

facts.fact: In 1965, India’s prime minister Lal Bahadur Shastri asked the country to skip one meal a week. India then imported 18,000 tonnes of Mexican wheat seed bred by Norman Borlaug’s team, and within a few years its wheat harvest reached 17 million tonnes. A newborn in India could expect about 46 years in 1966, and about 72 today.
facts.source: M. S. Swaminathan, ICAR interview · Orissa Review (2010) · UN World Population Prospects, via Our World in Data

facts.fact: Ultra-processed food is about a fifth of the calories people eat in Brazil (19.7%) and more than half in the United States (55%). Brazil’s official food guide says to choose fresh food and home-made meals over ultra-processed food, and to eat at regular times, with other people when you can. In most countries, more adults now live with obesity than are underweight.
facts.source: Louzada et al. (2023) · CDC NCHS Data Brief 536 · Dietary Guidelines for the Brazilian Population (2014) · NCD-RisC, Lancet (2024)

facts.fact: Food gave us years, but not alone: one study found clean water alone was behind nearly half the drop in deaths in big American cities in the early 1900s. Today about one in five deaths worldwide is linked to diet — mostly too much salt, too few whole grains and too little fruit. Life expectancy at birth, worldwide: about 29 in 1800, about 73 today.
facts.source: Cutler & Miller, Demography (2005) · GBD 2017 Diet Collaborators, Lancet (2019) · Riley (2005) · UN World Population Prospects 2024

episodes.commentPrompt: Which century’s kitchen would you eat in, and why?

episodes.title: Medicine
episodes.subject: Medicine
episodes.hook: In 1799, George Washington’s doctors drained, by some estimates, around two fifths of his blood. They were trained, and they meant well. So how did anyone ever find out what really works?
episodes.question: Did you know that in 1799 George Washington’s doctors drained, by some estimates, around two fifths of his blood?
episodes.guess: In 1948, 55 tuberculosis patients got a new drug and 52 got bed rest alone. After six months, how many of the 55 had died? Guess in the comments, then stay to the end and check.
episodes.summary: Seven mornings, seven patients: a gunshot wound in a French army camp near Turin, George Washington at Mount Vernon, a new mother in Vienna’s General Hospital, the first penicillin patient in Oxford, tuberculosis patients on a British ward, a child in Merca, Somalia, the town of the last natural smallpox case — and a 2100 scenario, clearly labelled, where the cures race the germs.

quiz.question: In 1948, 55 tuberculosis patients got streptomycin and 52 got bed rest alone. After six months, how many of the 55 had died?
quiz.reveal: Four of the 55 — against fourteen of the 52 who got bed rest alone. Chance decided who got the drug, and then everyone was counted.

questions.question: In an army camp near Turin in 1537, the boiling oil for gunshot wounds ran out. What did the surgeon Ambroise Paré use instead?
options: More boiling oil, from the next camp
A salve of egg yolk, rose oil and turpentine
questions.reveal: A plain salve of egg yolk, rose oil and turpentine. By his own account, those men slept better and their wounds swelled less — he wrote it up years later.

questions.question: On his last day in December 1799, how much blood did George Washington’s doctors take, by most counts?
options: More than 80 ounces — about two and a half litres
None — they refused to bleed him
questions.reveal: More than 80 ounces, about two and a half litres, over roughly twelve hours — by some estimates around two fifths of his blood. He died that night.

questions.question: Vienna’s General Hospital had two maternity clinics: one trained doctors, one trained midwives. In 1840–46, where did more mothers die?
options: In the doctors’ clinic — about 2.7 times as many
questions.reveal: In the doctors’ clinic: 98.4 deaths per 1,000 births, against 36.2 in the midwives’ clinic. The doctors came straight from the dissecting room.

questions.question: In April 1847, 18.3% of mothers in Semmelweis’s clinic died. He made everyone wash their hands in chlorinated lime. What was the rate in July?
questions.reveal: 1.2%. He picked chlorinated lime to get rid of the smell of dead tissue — nobody yet knew about germs. He counted, and the pattern spoke.

questions.question: In February 1941 in Oxford, a police officer was the first person treated with penicillin. He got better within a day. Why did he still die?
questions.reveal: The penicillin ran out. The team even recovered it from his urine to use again, but after five days it was gone, and he relapsed. The limit was the supply, not the idea.

questions.question: In the 1948 streptomycin trial, the drug was scarce. How was it decided which patients got it?
questions.reveal: Random sampling numbers in sealed envelopes — the doctors didn’t know who would get it. Then both groups were counted, fairly.

questions.question: Ali Maow Maalin of Merca, Somalia, was the last person to catch smallpox naturally, in 1977. How many human diseases have been wiped out so far?
questions.reveal: Just one: smallpox. Eradication was announced by the WHO on 8 May 1980. Ali Maow Maalin recovered and later worked to vaccinate against polio.

questions.question: Washington’s doctors trusted authority. What did Semmelweis and the 1948 trial do that changed medicine?
options: They compared a treated group with an untreated one, and counted
They asked the patients to vote
questions.reveal: They asked a simple question: compared with what? Semmelweis counted deaths before and after handwashing; the 1948 trial let chance decide and then counted. Medicine got better because it learned to test itself.

eras.line: Smoke, drums, and the groans of wounded men.
eras.saw: Balance. The body is a scale, and the doctor adjusts it.

eras.line: It’s December. Snow and sleet blow across the fields.
eras.saw: Authority. Trust the expert, even when the expert bleeds you.

eras.line: A cold morning on the maternity ward of the General Hospital.
eras.saw: Pattern. Count the deaths, then look for the cause.

eras.line: It’s wartime, and the lights are low.
eras.saw: A cure. A drug that finds the germ and leaves you alone.

eras.line: Patients with tuberculosis lie in rows. The only sound is coughing.
eras.saw: Proof. Don’t believe it. Test it, fairly.

eras.line: Fishing boats rest on the sand.
eras.saw: Prevention. Stop the disease before it starts.

eras.line: That morning hasn’t happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: In 1799, doctors trusted authority. In 2100, what will you trust?

facts.fact: In an army camp near Turin, the surgeon Ambroise Paré ran out of the boiling oil used on gunshot wounds and dressed them with egg yolk, rose oil and turpentine instead. By his own account, those men slept better and swelled less. Medicine then meant balance: four humours, and bleeding to set them right. In England, a newborn could expect about 35 years.
facts.source: Britannica and Delaware Academy of Medicine on Ambroise Paré · PMC1796715 on humoral theory · Wrigley & Schofield, via Our World in Data

facts.fact: On 14 December 1799, George Washington’s doctors bled him four times in about twelve hours: more than 80 ounces, about two and a half litres — by some estimates around two fifths of his blood. One doctor proposed a tracheotomy and was overruled. He died that night. Worldwide, a newborn in 1800 could expect about 29 years.
facts.source: Morens, Am Surg 2008 (PubMed 18705585) · Hektoen International · PBS NewsHour · UN/Riley via Our World in Data

facts.fact: Vienna’s General Hospital had two maternity clinics. In 1840–46, the First, which trained doctors, lost 98.4 mothers per 1,000 births; the Second, which trained midwives, lost 36.2. In 1846 the First Clinic’s rate was five times the Second’s.

In April 1847, 18.3% of mothers in Ignaz Semmelweis’s clinic died. From mid-May he made everyone wash in chlorinated lime: 2.2% in June, 1.2% in July, 1.9% in August. He chose it to remove the smell of dead tissue — germs weren’t understood yet. In Britain, a newborn could expect about 38 years.
facts.source: Semmelweis’s First Clinic figures, 1847 · PMC3807776 · Our World in Data

facts.fact: On 12 February 1941, Albert Alexander, an Oxford police officer, became the first patient treated with penicillin. He improved within a day, but the supply ran out after five days, even though the team recovered penicillin from his urine; he died on 15 March. In Britain, a newborn could expect about 61 years.
facts.source: University of Oxford, 75 years of penicillin in people · Hektoen International · Our World in Data

facts.fact: In the Medical Research Council’s 1948 trial, 55 tuberculosis patients got streptomycin and bed rest and 52 got bed rest alone, assigned by random numbers in sealed envelopes. In six months, 4 of the 55 died against 14 of the 52. In Britain, a newborn could expect about 68 years.
facts.source: BMJ 1948;2:769–782, via Senn, Dicing with Death, and Armitage · Our World in Data

facts.fact: Ali Maow Maalin, a hospital cook in Merca, Somalia, was the last person to catch smallpox naturally, in October 1977. He recovered. The WHO announced eradication on 8 May 1980 — the only human disease eradicated so far. Worldwide, a newborn can now expect about 73 years.
facts.source: WHO and NLM on smallpox eradication · UN World Population Prospects 2024

facts.fact: Medicine didn’t get better because doctors got smarter. It got better when someone asked: compared with what? Semmelweis counted deaths before and after handwashing; the 1948 trial let chance decide who got the drug, then counted. James Lind had compared six cures for scurvy in 1747.
facts.source: PMC3807776 · BMJ 1948 via Senn and Armitage · James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753), James Lind Library

episodes.commentPrompt: Which century’s doctor would you trust, and why?

episodes.title: Light
episodes.subject: Light
episodes.hook: In Britain, light now costs less than one three-thousandth of what it did in 1800. You’d think we’d pocket the savings. We didn’t. So what happened when we switched the night off?
episodes.question: Did you know that, at today’s rate, a child born where 250 stars are visible will see about 100 by the age of 18?
episodes.guess: Think of ten people anywhere on Earth. How many of them live under a night sky that our lights have brightened? Two? Five? More than eight? Guess in the comments, then stay to the end and check.
episodes.summary: Six evenings, six new ways to beat the dark: a rushlight and a curfew bell in a market town in Flanders, the first gas lamps on Pall Mall in London, kerosene and the first commercial oil well in Titusville, Pennsylvania, Edison’s Pearl Street Station lighting a few blocks of lower Manhattan, the blue LED made in Tokushima, Japan, and your own window tonight — and a 2100 scenario, clearly labelled, where the dark has to be protected.

quiz.question: Think of ten people anywhere on Earth. How many of them live under a night sky that our lights have brightened?
quiz.reveal: More than eight in ten — and in the United States and Europe, more than 99 people in 100. Every time light got cheaper, we used more, until it filled the sky.

questions.question: In a Flemish market town in 1500, an evening bell ends the day. It’s called the curfew. What does the word come from?
questions.reveal: “Cover the fire”, from the old French covrefeu. When the bell rang, you banked the hearth and the day was over.

questions.question: The economist William Nordhaus priced light in hours of work. In ancient Babylon, one ordinary bulb’s worth of light for an hour cost about 41.5 hours of work. What did it cost in America in 1800, with a tallow candle?
questions.reveal: About 5.4 hours of work. The price had fallen since Babylon, but light was still a luxury you made last.

questions.question: In June 1807, Frederick Winsor lit part of Pall Mall in London with coal gas. What was the public display for?
questions.reveal: King George III’s birthday, on 4 June 1807. In 1812, Parliament chartered the Gas Light and Coke Company, the world’s first gas company.

questions.question: After Edwin Drake struck oil at Titusville in 1859, kerosene filled the lamps. A 1938 history said oil gave kerosene to the world — and life to what?
questions.reveal: “Life to the few remaining whales.” The line is from Stotz’s 1938 gas-industry history, quoted by the economist William Nordhaus.

questions.question: On 4 September 1882, Edison’s Pearl Street Station lit a few blocks of lower Manhattan. Where was Edison when the lights came on?
options: At the switch in the power station
In the office of the banker J. P. Morgan
On a ship in the harbour
questions.reveal: In J. P. Morgan’s office, at Drexel, Morgan & Co., wired with about 106 lamps. An engineer on Pearl Street closed the switch, and about 400 lamps lit on day one.

questions.question: In 1993, Shuji Nakamura in Tokushima, Japan made the first high-brightness LED of the colour everyone was missing. Which colour?
questions.reveal: Blue. Red LEDs existed long before, but efficient blue LEDs made bright, energy-saving white light possible. Nakamura, Akasaki and Amano shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

questions.question: Go to your window tonight. The Milky Way is hidden from how much of humanity?
options: About one person in a hundred
questions.reveal: More than a third of humanity — 60% of Europeans and nearly 80% of North Americans.

questions.question: In Britain, from 1800 to 2000, light came to cost less than one three-thousandth as much. What did people do?
questions.reveal: Each person used about 6,500 times more light. We didn’t save the light; we spent it. In 1500, the scarce thing was light. Today, the scarce thing is the dark.

eras.line: It’s late autumn. The light is going, and the church bell starts to ring.
eras.saw: A luxury. You make it yourself, and you make it last.

eras.line: It’s a warm June evening, and a crowd is staring at a row of iron posts.
eras.saw: A service. It comes to you, through a pipe.

eras.line: It’s August. The air smells of mud and tar, and men are cheering around a wooden derrick.
eras.saw: A liquid. Something you buy in a can.

eras.line: It’s the fourth of September, a Monday afternoon. Horses, newspapers, the clatter of the street.
eras.saw: A network. You plug into a system you’ll never see.

eras.line: Inside a small company lab, an engineer is staring at a chip.
eras.saw: A crystal. Light without fire.

eras.line: Well, tonight. Count the lights you can see. Streetlights, signs, the office that never switches off.
eras.saw: Too cheap to switch off. Every time the price fell, we bought more.

eras.line: That morning hasn’t happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: In 1500, the bell meant cover the fire. In 2100, it might mean cover the light.

facts.fact: “Curfew” comes from the old French covrefeu, “cover the fire”: an evening bell told households to cover or bank the hearth. Most evenings were lit by tallow candles, made from animal fat, smoky and smelly, or by rushlights, a dried rush dipped in fat, lasting a few minutes to an hour. Beeswax cost several times more and went mainly to the church and the rich.
facts.source: Merriam-Webster and Etymonline on “curfew” · Gilbert White, via Wikipedia “Rushlight” · Johnston Collection, The art of lighting

facts.fact: William Nordhaus priced light in hours of work for 1,000 lumen-hours, about one ordinary bulb for an hour. A Babylonian sesame-oil lamp, around 1750 BC: 41.5 hours. A tallow candle in America in 1800: 5.4 hours.
facts.source: Nordhaus, The History of Lighting Suggests Not, in The Economics of New Goods (NBER, 1997), table 1.4

facts.fact: In June 1807, Frederick Albert Winsor lit part of Pall Mall in London with coal gas, with a public display for King George III’s birthday on 4 June; by the end of the year, 13 lamps lined the south side. In 1812, Parliament chartered the Gas Light and Coke Company, the world’s first gas company.
facts.source: Museum of London, Gas lamps illuminated London · London Remembers, 100 Pall Mall

facts.fact: In 1846, the Canadian Abraham Gesner distilled a lamp fuel from coal, sold as kerosene. On 27 August 1859, Edwin Drake struck oil at Titusville, Pennsylvania, 69 feet down. A 1938 history said petroleum “gave kerosene to the world, and life to the few remaining whales”. By 1870, an hour of light cost about 20 minutes of work.
facts.source: AOGHS, American oil history · Stotz (1938), quoted in Nordhaus (1997) · Nordhaus (1997), table 1.4

facts.fact: At about 3 p.m. on 4 September 1882, an engineer closed the switch at Edison’s Pearl Street Station. About 400 lamps lit up in a few blocks of lower Manhattan; Edison himself was at Drexel, Morgan & Co., J. P. Morgan’s office, wired with about 106 lamps. By 1900, an hour of light cost about 13 minutes of work.
facts.source: ETHW Milestone, Pearl Street Station 1882 · Nordhaus (1997), table 1.4

facts.fact: In 1993, Shuji Nakamura of Nichia in Tokushima, Japan, made the first high-brightness blue LED. With Akasaki and Amano he shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics, for efficient blue LEDs that enabled bright, energy-saving white light. In 1992, with a compact fluorescent bulb, an hour of light cost about 0.4 seconds of work.
facts.source: nobelprize.org, Physics 2014 · UCSB Materials · Nordhaus (1997), table 1.4

facts.fact: More than 80% of the world’s people, and more than 99% in the US and Europe, live under light-polluted skies. The Milky Way is hidden from more than a third of humanity, 60% of Europeans and nearly 80% of North Americans. Star counts by citizen scientists suggest the night sky is brightening by about 9.6% a year.
facts.source: Falchi et al., Science Advances 2016 · Kyba et al., Science 2023 (Globe at Night)

facts.fact: In Britain, from 1800 to 2000, lighting came to cost less than one three-thousandth as much. Each person used about 6,500 times more light, and the country 25,000 times more, while GDP per head rose about 15 times. We didn’t save the light; we spent it. In 1500, the scarce thing was light. Today, it’s the dark.
facts.source: Fouquet & Pearson, Energy Journal 27(1), 2006 · Our World in Data, price of lighting

episodes.commentPrompt: Streetlights or stars: if you had to give one up, which would it be, and why?

episodes.title: Weight
episodes.subject: Weight
episodes.hook: Twenty people check into a hospital. None of them is sick. Two menus, matched on the plate: same calories, same sugar, fat, salt and fibre. Eat as much as you want. One of the menus quietly made people eat far more. Why?
episodes.question: Did you know that two menus with the same calories on the plate can make people eat very different amounts?
episodes.guess: Two menus, the same calories on the plate, eat as much as you like. Did people eat the same amount of each? Guess in the comments, then watch and check.
episodes.summary: Medicine 1 of 10, a short explainer with one experiment and one mystery: twenty healthy adults on a hospital ward in Maryland, two menus matched on the plate, a nurse with a scale and a clock. Then the clues, the gut-to-brain signal that says “enough”, the honest limits, a 2025 test in England, and Bruegel’s two kitchens from 1563.
episodes.commentPrompt: Which menu would you pick: the cheaper, faster one, or the one cooked from scratch?

quiz.question: Two menus with the same calories on the plate, eat as much as you like. What happened?
options: People ate the same amount of each
A few more calories of the ultra-processed menu
About 500 calories a day more of the ultra-processed menu
quiz.reveal: About 500 calories a day more, without feeling any hungrier, and they didn’t like it better.

questions.question: Twenty people check into a hospital ward in Maryland. None of them is sick. How long do they get to eat each meal before a nurse takes the tray away?
questions.reveal: Up to an hour. Then the tray went away and staff weighed what was left, every meal, for four weeks.

questions.question: The two menus were matched on the plate. What was matched?
options: Calories, sugar, fat, salt and fibre
questions.reveal: Calories, sugar, fat, salt and fibre. On paper they were the same food; only the processing differed.

questions.question: After two weeks on the ultra-processed menu, what had happened to people’s weight?
questions.reveal: They gained about a kilo, and lost about a kilo on the other menu.

questions.question: So did people find the ultra-processed food tastier?
questions.reveal: About the same. They rated both menus about equally pleasant, and they weren’t hungrier either.

questions.question: The nurses timed every meal. How much faster did people eat on the ultra-processed menu?
questions.reveal: About 17 calories a minute faster. Faster and denser, with the same hunger.

questions.question: On the unprocessed menu, what did the “enough” hormone, PYY, do?
questions.reveal: It went up, and the “eat” hormone, ghrelin, went down.

questions.question: In 2025 a team in England tested two healthy diets, minimally processed versus ultra-processed. How did the minimally processed one do?
options: About ten times the weight loss
questions.reveal: About twice the weight loss: around 2% of body weight against 1%. Even a “healthy” processed menu lost out.

questions.question: In the first study, which week of food cost less?
questions.reveal: The ultra-processed week: about $106, against $151. The food that’s easiest to overeat was also the cheapest.

eras.line: Pieter Bruegel draws two kitchens: in one, people feast; in the other, they starve. Plenty is the dream.
Twenty people, four weeks, two menus matched on the plate. Eat as much as you want.
Fifty-five adults, two healthy diets, eight weeks each. Does the processing still matter?
One in seven people on Earth lives with obesity. The food that’s easiest to overeat is also the cheapest and the fastest.

facts.fact: Twenty healthy adults, ten men and ten women, checked into the NIH Clinical Center, a hospital research ward in Bethesda, Maryland. For four weeks every meal was served on a tray; they had up to an hour to eat, and staff weighed whatever was left.
facts.source: Hall KD et al., Cell Metabolism 30(1):67–77, 2019 (NIH Clinical Center inpatient trial)

facts.fact: The two menus were matched as served for calories, energy density, sugar, fat, salt and fibre. Only the processing differed: two weeks ultra-processed, two weeks unprocessed, in random order.
facts.source: Hall KD et al., Cell Metabolism 30(1):67–77, 2019 (NIH Clinical Center inpatient trial)

facts.fact: On the ultra-processed menu people ate about 500 more calories a day (508 ± 106 kcal). In two weeks they gained about 0.9 kg; on the unprocessed menu they lost about 0.9 kg.
facts.source: Hall KD et al., Cell Metabolism 30(1):67–77, 2019 (NIH Clinical Center inpatient trial)

facts.fact: They rated both menus about equally pleasant and familiar, and they were no hungrier on either. The extra calories didn’t come from better taste.
facts.source: Hall KD et al., Cell Metabolism 30(1):67–77, 2019 (NIH Clinical Center inpatient trial)

facts.fact: Every meal was timed. On the ultra-processed menu people ate faster: about 17 more calories a minute. Bite for bite, the ultra-processed food (drinks aside) was also far denser in calories.
facts.source: Hall KD et al., Cell Metabolism 30(1):67–77, 2019 (NIH Clinical Center inpatient trial)

facts.fact: On the unprocessed menu the fullness hormone PYY rose and the hunger hormone ghrelin fell, compared with the start. The researchers’ best explanation: fast, calorie-dense food outruns the signal that says “enough”. They say the exact cause is still open.
facts.source: Hall KD et al., Cell Metabolism 30(1):67–77, 2019 (NIH Clinical Center inpatient trial)

facts.fact: In England, 55 adults ate two healthy diets that both followed the UK’s Eatwell Guide, eight weeks each. Both led to weight loss, but the minimally processed one did about twice as well: around 2% of body weight, against about 1%.
facts.source: Dicken SJ et al., Nature Medicine, 2025, doi 10.1038/s41591-025-03842-0

facts.fact: In the 2019 study the ultra-processed week was the cheaper one: about $106 a week against $151 for the unprocessed menu, at 2,000 calories a day and US supermarket prices.
facts.source: Hall KD et al., Cell Metabolism 30(1):67–77, 2019 (NIH Clinical Center inpatient trial)

episodes.title: Diabetes
episodes.subject: Diabetes
episodes.hook: Toronto, 1921. A dog with no pancreas lives for seventy days on an extract. Then a dying boy gets the same kind of shot, and it almost does nothing. Why?
episodes.question: Did you know that the first insulin injection ever given to a person almost did nothing?
episodes.guess: The first shot almost did nothing. Twelve days later came a cleaner one. Did it work? Guess in the comments, then watch and check.
episodes.summary: Medicine 2 of 10, a short explainer with one story and one mystery: a Toronto lab in 1921, a dog the lab called Dog 33, and Leonard Thompson, 14, whose first injection almost did nothing. Then the clue in the jar, what insulin actually does, why it isn’t a cure, the type 2 twist, and a one-dollar patent. This isn’t medical advice: if diabetes is part of your life, talk to a doctor who knows you.
episodes.commentPrompt: Would you have tried the second injection, after the first one almost did nothing?

quiz.question: A dying boy’s first injection almost did nothing. Twelve days later he got a cleaner extract. What happened?
options: His blood sugar fell a little more
His blood sugar fell to normal
quiz.reveal: His blood sugar fell from about 520 to 120 mg/dL, normal, and the ketones disappeared.

questions.question: In November 1921, Dog 33, later called Marjorie, started injections of a pancreas extract. How long was she kept alive on them?
questions.reveal: Seventy days. The lab records number the dogs; the name Marjorie came later.

questions.question: 11 January 1922: Leonard Thompson, 14, gets the first injection. What happens?
options: His blood sugar falls to normal
His blood sugar falls only a little, and an abscess grows
questions.reveal: It fell only a little, from 0.440% to 0.320%. The ketones stayed, and impurities in the extract caused an abscess.

questions.question: The biochemist James Collip cleaned up the extract. How?
options: He kept adding alcohol, past 90%, until the active part fell out of the liquid
He froze it and thawed it again
questions.reveal: He raised the alcohol concentration past 90% until the active part precipitated, falling out of the liquid on its own.

questions.question: How many days after the first shot did Leonard get the cleaner extract?
questions.reveal: Twelve: on 23 January 1922. His blood sugar fell from 0.520% to 0.120%, about 520 to 120 mg/dL, normal, and the ketones disappeared.

questions.question: The insulin patent was assigned to the University of Toronto. For how much?
questions.reveal: One dollar, once. The assignment was signed on 19 December 1922.

questions.question: Which cells in the pancreas make insulin?
questions.reveal: Beta cells, in the islets. In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys them.

questions.question: Does insulin cure type 1 diabetes?
options: No: it keeps people alive, but it isn’t a cure
questions.reveal: No. People with type 1 diabetes need insulin to survive, one dose at a time; it isn’t a cure.

questions.question: How much of all diabetes today is type 2?
questions.reveal: Over 90%. In type 2 the body doesn’t use insulin properly.

eras.line: Banting and Best start work in May. In November, Dog 33 begins the injections and is kept alive on them for seventy days.
Leonard Thompson, 14, gets the first injection. His blood sugar falls only a little.
Twelve days later, a cleaner extract. His blood sugar falls to normal.
589 million adults live with diabetes, about 1 in 9, and more than 4 in 10 of them don’t know it.

facts.fact: In November 1921, in a Toronto university lab, Dog 33 began injections of a pancreas extract and was kept alive on them for 70 days. The lab records number the dogs; the name Marjorie came later.
facts.source: U of T Fisher Library, The Discovery of Insulin at the University of Toronto (2021), “Photograph of Dog 33”; Lambert & Delgado, Biomedicines 12(3):533, 2024

facts.fact: On 11 January 1922 Leonard Thompson, 14, got the first injection. His blood sugar fell only a little, from 0.440% to 0.320%; the ketones stayed, and impurities in the extract caused an abscess.
facts.source: U of T Fisher Library, The Discovery of Insulin at the University of Toronto (2021), “From Embarrassment to Triumph” and “Leonard Thompson”

facts.fact: The biochemist James Collip purified the extract by raising the alcohol concentration past 90% until the active part precipitated.
facts.source: U of T Fisher Library, The Discovery of Insulin at the University of Toronto (2021), “From Embarrassment to Triumph”; Science History Institute

facts.fact: On 23 January 1922, twelve days after the first shot, Leonard got the cleaner extract. His blood sugar fell from 0.520% to 0.120%, about 520 to 120 mg/dL, normal, and the ketones disappeared.
facts.source: U of T Fisher Library, The Discovery of Insulin at the University of Toronto (2021), “From Embarrassment to Triumph” (reporting Banting et al., CMAJ 12(3):141–146, 1922)

facts.fact: The insulin patent was assigned to the Governors of the University of Toronto for one dollar, once. The assignment was signed on 19 December 1922 and recorded on 1 January 1923.
facts.source: U of T Fisher Library, The Discovery of Insulin at the University of Toronto (2021), document 7143, “Assignment to the Governors of the University of Toronto”

facts.fact: Islets in the pancreas hold beta cells that make insulin. Insulin helps glucose get from the blood into cells, to be used for energy. In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys those beta cells.
facts.source: NIDDK, “What is diabetes?” and “Type 1 diabetes”

facts.fact: Insulin keeps people with type 1 diabetes alive, but it isn’t a cure. Leonard Thompson lived thirteen more years and died in 1935, aged 27, of pneumonia.
facts.source: WHO diabetes fact sheet; NIDDK, “Type 1 diabetes”; U of T Fisher Library, The Discovery of Insulin at the University of Toronto (2021), “Leonard Thompson”

facts.fact: Over 90% of diabetes is type 2, where the body doesn’t use insulin properly.
facts.source: International Diabetes Federation, “Diabetes facts & figures” (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th edition, 2025); WHO diabetes fact sheet
